title: Metals and Non-Metals
content:
# Metals and Non-Metals

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
- Describe the typical properties of metals and non-metals
- Explain the properties of metals in terms of structure and bonding
- Identify metals and non-metals from their properties
- Explain what metalloids are and give examples

## Introduction

The elements in the Periodic Table can be broadly classified as **metals** or **non-metals** based on their physical and chemical properties. About 80% of elements are metals. Understanding the differences between metals and non-metals helps us predict how they will behave.

## Key Concepts

### Properties of Metals

Most metals share these typical properties:

**Physical Properties:**

| Property | Description |
|----------|-------------|
| Lustrous | Shiny when polished |
| Good conductors | Conduct heat and electricity well |
| Malleable | Can be hammered into sheets |
| Ductile | Can be drawn into wires |
| High melting/boiling points | Most are solid at room temperature (except mercury) |
| High density | Generally dense materials |
| Sonorous | Make a ringing sound when struck |

**Chemical Properties:**
- Form positive ions (cations) by losing electrons
- React with oxygen to form basic oxides
- React with acids to form salts and hydrogen

**Examples:** Iron (Fe), Copper (Cu), Aluminium (Al), Gold (Au), Sodium (Na)

### Properties of Non-Metals

Non-metals have contrasting properties:

**Physical Properties:**

| Property | Description |
|----------|-------------|
| Dull | Not shiny (except graphite and iodine) |
| Poor conductors | Insulators of heat and electricity (except graphite) |
| Brittle | Shatter when hammered (if solid) |
| Not ductile | Cannot be drawn into wires |
| Low melting/boiling points | Often gases or low-melting solids at room temperature |
| Low density | Generally light materials |

**Chemical Properties:**
- Form negative ions (anions) by gaining electrons, or share electrons
- React with oxygen to form acidic oxides
- Do not react with dilute acids

**Examples:** Oxygen (O), Carbon (C), Nitrogen (N), Sulfur (S), Chlorine (Cl)

### Comparison Table

| Property | Metals | Non-Metals |
|----------|--------|------------|
| Electrical conductivity | Good | Poor (except graphite) |
| Thermal conductivity | Good | Poor |
| Appearance | Shiny (lustrous) | Dull |
| Malleability | Malleable | Brittle |
| State at room temp | Mostly solid | Solid, liquid, or gas |
| Ion formation | Positive ions (+) | Negative ions (-) |
| Oxide type | Basic | Acidic |
| Position in Periodic Table | Left and centre | Right |

### Why Metals Have These Properties

The properties of metals are explained by **metallic bonding**:

- Metal atoms lose their outer electrons
- These electrons become delocalised (free to move throughout the structure)
- Positive metal ions are held in a "sea" of delocalised electrons

[DIAGRAM: Metallic bonding showing positive ions surrounded by delocalised electrons]

**Explaining properties:**
- **Electrical conductivity:** Delocalised electrons can move and carry charge
- **Thermal conductivity:** Delocalised electrons transfer energy quickly
- **Malleability/ductility:** Layers of ions can slide over each other without breaking

### Metalloids (Semi-metals)

**Metalloids** are elements with properties of both metals and non-metals. They are found along the stepped line in the Periodic Table.

**Examples:** Silicon (Si), Germanium (Ge), Arsenic (As), Boron (B)

**Properties of metalloids:**
- Intermediate electrical conductivity (semiconductors)
- Can be shiny or dull
- Usually brittle
- Conduct electricity better at higher temperatures

**Important use:** Silicon and germanium are used in electronic components (computer chips, solar cells) because they are semiconductors.

### Location in the Periodic Table

[DIAGRAM: Periodic Table showing metals, non-metals, and metalloids]

- **Metals:** Left side and centre (most of the table)
- **Non-metals:** Upper right corner
- **Metalloids:** Along the stepped line dividing metals and non-metals
- **Hydrogen:** Special case - a non-metal placed with Group 1

## Practical Applications

**Metals are used for:**
- Electrical wiring (copper) - good conductor
- Construction (steel/iron) - strong and malleable
- Jewellery (gold, silver) - lustrous and unreactive
- Cooking pans (aluminium, copper) - good thermal conductors

**Non-metals are used for:**
- Insulators (rubber, plastic) - poor conductors
- Fuels (carbon compounds) - release energy when burned
- Packaging (plastics) - light and mouldable

**Metalloids are used for:**
- Computer chips (silicon) - semiconductor properties
- Solar cells (silicon, germanium) - convert light to electricity

## Common Mistakes

- **Mistake:** Thinking all metals are hard and strong
- **Correct:** Some metals are soft (sodium can be cut with a knife) and some have low melting points (mercury is liquid at room temperature)

- **Mistake:** Thinking all non-metals are gases
- **Correct:** Non-metals can be solids (carbon, sulfur), liquids (bromine), or gases (oxygen, nitrogen)

- **Mistake:** Saying carbon conducts electricity, so it's a metal
- **Correct:** Only graphite (a form of carbon) conducts; diamond doesn't. Carbon is a non-metal with unusual properties.

## Practice Questions

1. State three physical properties of metals. (3 marks)

2. Explain why metals are good conductors of electricity. (3 marks)

3. Explain why non-metals are generally poor conductors of electricity. (2 marks)

4. Element X has the following properties: solid at room temperature, shiny appearance, conducts electricity, forms positive ions.
   State whether X is a metal or non-metal, giving reasons for your answer. (3 marks)

5. Silicon is described as a metalloid. Explain what this means and give one use of silicon based on its properties. (3 marks)

6. Explain, in terms of structure, why metals are malleable but non-metals are brittle. (4 marks)

## Key Terms Glossary

| Term | Definition |
|------|------------|
| Metal | An element that is typically shiny, conducts electricity, and forms positive ions |
| Non-metal | An element that is typically dull, does not conduct electricity, and may form negative ions |
| Metalloid | An element with properties between metals and non-metals |
| Malleable | Can be hammered into shape without breaking |
| Ductile | Can be drawn into wires |
| Lustrous | Having a shiny appearance |
| Delocalised electrons | Electrons that are free to move throughout a metal structure |
| Semiconductor | A material with electrical conductivity between a conductor and an insulator |

## Summary

- Metals are typically shiny, conduct heat and electricity, and are malleable and ductile
- Non-metals are typically dull, poor conductors, and brittle if solid
- Metal properties are explained by delocalised electrons in metallic bonding
- Metalloids have properties of both metals and non-metals
- Metals form positive ions; non-metals form negative ions
- Metals are on the left of the Periodic Table; non-metals on the right
